entries.b: Her coaching method in three moves. Regulate the nervous system first, then rewire the programs and beliefs, then rise into the identity of who you are becoming.

“Identity” is the most-used idea across the Breakthrough calls. Be, Do, Have: become them by doing what they do, and you will have what they have. The DO is the staircase that closes the gap to the future self.

Your reticular activating system filters about 11 million bits of information down to 126 bits a second, filtering on your values, programs and beliefs. The Proof Portfolio collects good proof on purpose so it outweighs the old proof your brain has been collecting.

Warm, direct, funny and a bit sweary. Australian spelling. Casual, run-on, conversational sentences with “like” and “right?”, tangents and self-interruptions when she talks; short punchy lines for emphasis. Uses ellipses. Swears less in scripts than live. High-achieving neurodivergent people (ADHD, autism, AuDHD). Identity work, brain rewiring, releasing repressed emotions, nervous system regulation and mindset. She previously ran a six-figure interior design studio.

Reflection questions:
• Where have you been neglecting your responsibility to take care of your body? (It’s okay, we’ve all been there. This is about being thankful for your body and brain, then worshipping it by starting to nourish it and take care of it just 1% better tomorrow.)

entries.t: Week 2 · The Foundations · Lesson 2: Conscious + Unconscious Mind

Reflection questions:
• What’s something you consciously want to do or achieve that you feel your unconscious mind keeps sabotaging? And for what purpose do you feel it’s stopping you? (What’s it trying to protect you from?) (This is going to help you uncover some patterns that will be useful to know for future lessons.)
• What are some of your unconscious habits you would like to change? (The things you do on autopilot.) (For me, it’s reaching for a sugary snack when I’m bored, or scratching my skin when I’m uncomfortable or concentrating.)
• Did any of these beliefs ring true for you? What other beliefs have you collected over the years that aren’t serving you? Jot down anything that comes to mind. (For me, in the past they all hit true, and I’m grateful to say I’m overcoming them all using the processes you’re going to learn in this program.)
• What shitty situation are you staying in just because it’s familiar? (But it’s actually keeping you stuck out of fear of change?) (I’ve stayed in relationships, jobs, careers, houses and bloody cities way too long because it was “known”, and that was easier than leaning into new, uncomfortable situations that could likely lead to a better life.)

• Do you believe your vagal tone is high (less reactive to stimulation) or low (more reactive to stimulation)? (Think about the last time you blew up over a lot happening at once. What tipped you over the edge? How much had accumulated? What did you need to do earlier in the day to avoid it? Was it the stacking effect, more than the things themselves?)
• What bodily messages has your brain been sending you that you may not have realised were a warning sign? (Headaches: thinking too much and not drinking enough water? Aching back: sitting too long, or what are you pushing to the back? Tummy aches: how long have you been stressed and repressing your emotions? That’s all held in the gut.)

entries.t: Week 2 · The Foundations · Lesson 6: Fight or Flight
entries.b:
Knowing what your states are, in what situations, and around which people you tend to use each one, is super helpful for changing the way you respond. Sometimes just becoming aware of it is enough.

Reflection questions:
• Have you been in fight or flight for a while now? Shutdown, burnout? Could the stress you’ve experienced have landed you in a shutdown state so your nervous system can rest? (It’s okay. I’ve been there, and it’s exactly why you’re in this course right now. I’ve got you!)
• Which state tends to be your default: fight, flight, freeze or fawn? (Defensive, avoidant, shut down or people-pleasing.) In what situations, and around which people? (You can be a range. With my husband I was more defensive because I felt safer to be me. With friends I was more people-pleasing or avoidant, and with strangers I was a freeze operator. Sometimes just becoming aware of it is enough.)
Little pockets of slow so your nervous system can catch up. Build your own pause menu.

Keys to a happy body: it might not be easy, but it is simple!

🔑 Drink water
🔑 Eat more energy than you burn (and regularly)
🔑 Move your body (we weren’t designed to be stationary beings)
🔑 Rest: your eyes after screens, your brain after thinking hard, your legs after running
🔑 Sleep: a good night-time routine, no screens, read to tire your eyes, empty your mind into a journal

Your body sends signals. Headaches, an aching back, tummy troubles, tight shoulders, a clenched jaw, a stiff neck, tired eyes, sore feet, aching hands, trouble sleeping, exhaustion: each has a practical side (water, posture, screens, sleep) and a question worth asking (What am I carrying? What am I avoiding? Where do I need more support?).

You don’t have to force a meaning. Sometimes an aching back needs a different chair, and sometimes the question about support opens an important conversation. Both deserve attention.

Reflection questions:

Clenched jaw: what words are you biting back? Sore feet: are you letting yourself move at your own pace? You don’t have to force a meaning. Sometimes an aching back just needs a different chair.)

entries.t: Week 3 · The Reality Framework · Lesson 4: Beliefs
entries.b:
❤️ Before you begin: your wellbeing comes first.

These questions may bring up difficult memories or emotions. You don’t need to revisit, describe or share traumatic experiences to benefit from this. Keep things at a level that feels manageable, skip any question, or stop altogether. There’s nothing to prove by pushing through distress.

This program offers education, coaching and self-reflection. It is not therapy, trauma treatment or a substitute for personalised mental health care.

If you feel overwhelmed, disconnected or unsafe, pause. Look around, notice your surroundings, feel your feet on the floor, and reach out to someone you trust.

If you have thoughts of self-harm or suicide, stop and get support straight away. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14 (24/7) or text 0477 13 11 14. If you’re in immediate danger, call 000. Outside Australia, contact your local crisis line or emergency number. Program messages are not a crisis service, so please don’t wait for a reply from me to get help.

Reflection questions:
• Childhood conditioning: what sort of behaviour was or wasn’t modelled to you growing up? (Money, confidence, self-worth, love, communication, values, behaviour. What do you catch yourself thinking or doing and wonder why? Likely you picked it up from what was modelled to you.)
• Reflect on the significant people you looked up to or grew up around. What behaviours did they pass to you? What was their upbringing like? (This isn’t about blame. They likely did the best they could with the resources they had. Just notice, note it down and leave it be for now.)
• What limiting beliefs have you collected over your life from past “trauma”, negative memories or labels given to you? (Go gentle here. You don’t need to go to the depths of anything that doesn’t feel safe. Examples: “I’m not a confident person.” “Travelling isn’t safe.” “I’m socially awkward because I’m autistic.” “I’m ADHD, so I can’t focus.” Each of these is a choice of belief, and there are empowering ones you can hold instead.)

How it works: Your exhale is the brake pedal
entries.b: Your vagus nerve runs from your brain stem down past your heart, lungs and gut. It is the main nerve of your rest and digest system. Every time you breathe in, your heart speeds up a tiny bit. Every time you breathe out, your vagus nerve gently slows it down. So when you make your exhale longer than your inhale, you press the brake for longer, your heart rate drops, and your brain gets the message: we are safe, we can stand down.

entries.t: How it works: The vagus nerve runs right past your voice box
entries.b: Branches of your vagus nerve control the muscles of your throat and voice box. Humming, singing and chanting gently activate those muscles and vibrate the area, and they also force a long, slow exhale. Long exhale plus vibration is a double dose of rest and digest. Humming also boosts nitric oxide in your sinuses, which helps air flow.

entries.t: How it works: Slow, gentle touch is a safety signal
entries.b: Your skin has special nerve fibres (C-tactile fibres) that respond best to slow, gentle stroking. They send signals to the parts of your brain that process emotion and safety, not just touch. Warm, caring touch, even your own, can lower stress hormones and release oxytocin, the bonding and calm chemical. It also pulls your attention out of your head and into your body.

entries.t: How it works: Deep pressure tells your nervous system it is held
entries.b: Firm, even pressure on your body (a weighted blanket, a big hug, a firm massage) stimulates pressure receptors deep in your skin and muscles. Deep pressure stimulation is linked with a shift towards rest and digest: a slower heart rate and a calmer, more organised feeling. Many neurodivergent people find it especially regulating, which is why it is used in occupational therapy.

entries.t: How it works: Your senses pull you into the present
entries.b: When you are stuck in your head, your brain is running on old stories and future worries. Your senses only work in the present moment. When you deliberately notice what you can see, hear, smell, taste and feel, you shift your brain’s attention from the overthinking loop to real, right-now information. That tells your nervous system: nothing dangerous is happening right here, right now. Smell is extra powerful because it goes straight to your brain’s emotion centre.

entries.t: How it works: Moving completes the stress cycle
entries.b: Stress hormones like adrenaline and cortisol are designed to get you moving: to fight or run. When you are stressed but stay still, those chemicals hang around in your body. Moving gives that energy somewhere to go and tells your body the threat is over, so the stress response can complete its cycle. Movement also releases endorphins and gives your brain proprioception, the sense of where your body is in space, which is very grounding.

entries.t: How it works: Nature gives your brain a soft kind of attention
entries.b: Screens and to-do lists demand hard, focused attention, which tires your brain out. Nature gives you soft fascination: the clouds, leaves and water hold your attention gently, so the overworked thinking part of your brain gets to rest. Studies on time in green spaces show lower cortisol, lower heart rate and better mood. Being outside also adds natural light, fresh air and movement, all good for your nervous system.

entries.t: How it works: Busy hands, quiet mind
entries.b: Rhythmic, repetitive work with your hands (stitching, colouring, kneading, shaping) fills up your brain’s working memory with something gentle, so there is less room for worry to loop. It can bring on flow, that absorbed state where time disappears. The steady rhythm itself is soothing to your nervous system, and the textures give you lots of grounding sensory input.

entries.t: How it works: Watching your thoughts instead of being them
entries.b: Your prefrontal cortex is the calm, wise part of your brain that can notice what is going on. Your amygdala is your smoke alarm. When you practise noticing thoughts (“hmm, interesting”) instead of following them, you strengthen the connection between the two, so your smoke alarm settles faster next time. Writing worries down does something similar: it moves them out of your working memory and onto the page.

entries.t: How it works: Warmth feels like safety
entries.b: Warmth on your skin widens your blood vessels and helps your muscles let go. Your brain links physical warmth with comfort and social connection (warm hands, a warm drink, a warm bath are all early safety signals from when you were tiny). Slowing down to notice the warmth also brings your attention into your body and into the present.

entries.t: How it works: Cold switches on your dive reflex
entries.b: When cold water hits your face (especially around your eyes and cheeks), your body triggers the mammalian dive reflex: an old survival response that slows your heart rate to save oxygen, like a seal diving underwater. Your vagus nerve does the slowing. That is why cold is one of the DBT “TIPP” skills therapists teach for moments when your emotions are at a 10. Cold on your hands, wrists or neck is gentler, but the strong sensation still pulls your attention straight into your body.

entries.t: How it works: A big sensation breaks the loop
entries.b: In panic or freeze, your brain gets stuck on a loop of danger signals. A big, sharp sensation (super sour, icy cold, a strong smell) or a task that takes real brain effort is too loud for your brain to ignore. It grabs your attention, and every bit of attention spent on the sour or the counting is attention not spent feeding the panic. It also gives your thinking brain something to do, which helps it come back online.

entries.t: How it works: Rhythm is regulating
entries.b: Steady, repetitive rhythm (rocking, swaying, tapping left and right) is one of the first ways a nervous system learns to calm down. It is how babies get settled. Rhythm is predictable, and predictable tells your brain it is safe. Stimming is your body doing this on purpose to regulate itself, so let it. Tapping both sides of your body in turn (like the butterfly hug) is also used in trauma therapy to help calm big feelings.

entries.t: How it works: Less input means more room
entries.b: A meltdown happens when more is coming in than your nervous system can process. You can’t calm down while the input keeps pouring in, so the first move is always to turn it down: less light, less noise, less talking, fewer demands. That stops the bucket from filling while your body catches up. Your brain finally gets space to process what has already come in, and that is when the calm can start.

entries.t: How it works: Safe people calm your nervous system
entries.b: Humans are built to calm down together. It is called co-regulation: a calm, safe voice or face can settle your nervous system faster than you can settle it alone. The part of your vagus nerve linked to safety is also tied to your face, your voice and your hearing, which is why a familiar, calm voice can be so soothing. You don’t have to explain anything. Just being connected to someone safe helps.

How: First inhale.: A slow, deep breath in through your nose, filling your lungs as much as is comfortable. Second inhale.: At the very top, take a second short, sharp sniff in through your nose to fully expand your lungs. Long exhale.: Slowly and completely breathe out through your mouth, like you’re fogging up a mirror. Make it longer than the inhale. Repeat 1 to 3 times.: Then breathe normally and notice the difference.

Why it works: Reinflates the air sacs in your lungs.: When you’re stressed, some of the tiny air sacs (alveoli) can partly collapse. The second inhale pops them back open. Offloads carbon dioxide.: The long exhale clears out extra carbon dioxide, which is part of what makes you feel panicky. Proven to work fast.: A Stanford study found five minutes a day of cyclic sighing improved mood and lowered breathing rate, more than mindfulness meditation did.

Helps with: Fast reset in under a minute, Slows your heart rate, Nobody can tell you’re doing it

When: During anxiety or panic, After being startled, Before a hard conversation, Before bed

How: Get comfortable.: Sitting or lying down. Put your hands on the sides of your ribs if you like. Breathe into your sides and back.: A little deeper than usual. Feel your ribs widen out under your hands, like an umbrella opening. Let it go slowly.: Breathe out gently and feel your ribs close back in. Keep going for a minute.: Five or six slow breaths is plenty.

Why it works: Uses your diaphragm properly.: Stressed breathing lives up in your chest and shoulders. Rib breathing brings your diaphragm back into the job, which is how your body breathes when it feels safe. Slower breathing, calmer heart.: Deeper breaths mean fewer breaths per minute, which shifts you towards rest and digest.

Helps with: Loosens a tight chest, Helps you fall asleep, Builds a calmer breathing habit

When: Lying in bed at night, When your chest feels tight, Waiting rooms and queues

Why it works: Gives your brain a job.: Counting and tracing keeps your attention busy, so it’s harder for anxious thoughts to take over. Steadies your breathing rhythm.: An even, slow rhythm brings your breathing and heart rate back into a calmer pattern.

Helps with: Steady and predictable, Great when your mind is racing, Used by first responders under pressure

When: Before a meeting or exam, When your thoughts are racing, When you need to focus

How: Hands on your thighs.: Palms flat, wherever you are sitting. Stroke slowly down to your knees.: Notice the fabric, the warmth and the pressure under your palms. Back up again.: Slowly. Slow is the magic part. Repeat for 30 seconds.: Breathe out a little longer while you do it.

Why it works: Slow stroking speaks the language of safety.: The nerve fibres that signal comfort respond best to slow, gentle strokes like this one. Brings you back into your body.: Your attention moves from your head to the feeling in your hands and legs.

Helps with: Invisible under a desk, Calms you in seconds, Grounds you in meetings

Notice the details.: The little ridges of your fingerprints, which fingers feel warmer, the pulse in your fingertips. Go back the other way.: Slowly, with a long breath out.

Why it works: Your fingertips are packed with nerve endings.: That gives your brain a lot of clear, present-moment information to focus on. A tiny focus task.: Moving finger by finger is just enough of a job to interrupt a thought spiral.

Helps with: Completely invisible, Quick focus reset, Works anywhere

When: On public transport, When you start to drift off, Mid-conversation overwhelm

How: Stand up.: Feet hip-width apart. Watch the reel and follow along.: Do it with me, as big or small as you like. Notice your energy before and after.: Rate it out of 10 at the start and the end.

Why it works: Wakes up your body fast.: Quick movement gets your blood pumping and sends more oxygen to your brain. Shifts you out of flat or freeze.: Movement tells your nervous system it’s time to come back online.

Helps with: More energy in two minutes, Clears brain fog, Fun, so you’ll actually do it

When: Afternoon slump, Before you start a task, When you feel flat or foggy

How: Thumb into your palm.: Make slow, firm circles in the centre of one palm with the other thumb. Squeeze each finger.: From the base to the tip, one at a time. Swap hands.: Give the other hand the same love. Add hand cream if you have it.: The smell and the slip make it even better.

Why it works: Hands are sensory hotspots.: A large part of the touch area in your brain is dedicated to your hands, so this sends a lot of grounding signals. Releases built-up tension.: We hold stress in our hands without noticing. Firm pressure helps the muscles let go.

Helps with: Calming and self-soothing, Eases tense, achy hands, Feels like a mini treat

When: After lots of typing, Watching TV at night, When you feel anxious

How: Plant both feet.: Flat on the floor, if you can. Press down.: Push your feet into the ground and feel the floor push back. Notice the details.: Your shoes, your socks, the weight of your body, the temperature. Wiggle your toes.: Then take one slow breath.

Why it works: Your feet are a long way from your head.: Literally moving your attention down your body moves you out of your thoughts. Feeling held by the ground.: Noticing that something solid is holding you up is a simple, powerful safety signal.

Helps with: Instant grounding, Totally invisible, Works during panic

When: Panic or anxiety, Hard conversations, Waiting for news

How: Hear.: Name one thing you can hear, in detail. See.: Name one thing you can see. Its colour, shape, how the light hits it. Smell.: One thing you can smell, even if it’s faint. Taste and feel.: One thing you can taste, and one thing you can feel on your skin.

Why it works: All five senses only work in the present.: So checking in with them drags your attention out of past and future worries and into right now. Detail matters.: The more detail you notice, the more your brain has to process, and the less room is left for the spiral.

Helps with: Out of your head fast, Anywhere, any time, Builds the habit of noticing

When: Stuck in your head, Before switching tasks, Waking up anxious
tags: Your senses pull you into the present

entries.b:
How: 5 things you can see.: Look around and name them. 4 things you can feel.: Your clothes, the chair, the air, your hair on your neck. 3 things you can hear.: Near and far. 2 things you can smell, 1 you can taste.: Then take a long breath out.

Why it works: Counting down gives structure.: When your brain is flooded, a simple countdown is easy to follow and gives you a clear task. Floods your brain with present-moment data.: Fifteen real things around you are hard to argue with: you’re here, now, and safe.

Helps with: Interrupts panic, Easy to remember, Used by therapists worldwide

When: Panic or a flashback, Spiralling thoughts, Overwhelm in a busy place
tags: Your senses pull you into the present

entries.b:
How: Lick your lips.: Notice how they feel. Take a small sip.: Hold it in your mouth for a moment. Really taste it.: The temperature, the flavour, the texture. Swallow slowly.: Feel it go all the way down.

Why it works: Swallowing is a rest and digest action.: Your vagus nerve is involved in swallowing, and your body only bothers with digesting when it feels safe. Taste is fully in the present.: It gives your brain a strong, simple focus point.

Helps with: Ten-second reset, Socially invisible, Calms your throat and gut

When: In meetings, When your mouth goes dry with nerves, At your desk
tags: Your senses pull you into the present

entries.b:
How: Pick three things.: Anything around you. Narrate like a nature documentary.: “And here we see the green mug, slightly chipped, glowing in the afternoon light…” Go into detail.: Colour, shape, texture, size, sound. In your head is fine.: Out loud if you want the giggle.

Why it works: Describing beats ruminating.: Putting real things into words uses the language part of your brain for the present instead of the worry. Humour helps.: A silly voice in your head makes it hard to keep spiralling, and a laugh is a quick nervous system reset.

Helps with: Breaks a thought loop, Makes you smile, Trains your noticing

When: Spiralling thoughts, Boredom-anxiety, Waiting around
tags: Your senses pull you into the present

entries.b:
How: Get something warm.: A mug of something, or warm running water. Wrap both hands around it.: Or let the warm water run over your hands and wrists. Feel all of it.: The heat, the weight, the texture of the mug. Breathe in the steam.: Slow breaths, longer out than in.

Why it works: Warmth relaxes your blood vessels and muscles.: Cold, tense hands are a sign of stress. Warming them sends the opposite message. A built-in comfort signal.: Your brain links warmth on your hands with care and safety.

Helps with: Cosy and comforting, Warms cold, stressed hands, Easy to make a ritual

When: Cold mornings, After bad news, Evening wind-down

How: Roll back three times.: Big, slow circles, lifting up towards your ears and down your back. Roll forward three times.: Same again, the other way. Drop them.: Let your shoulders fall as low as they’ll go. Unclench your jaw.: Teeth apart, tongue resting on the bottom of your mouth.

Why it works: Releases stress you’re holding.: Shoulders creep up and jaws clench when you’re stressed. Moving them tells your body it can let go. Your body talks to your brain.: Relaxed muscles send relaxed signals back up to your brain.

Helps with: Eases neck and shoulder tension, Works at your desk, Thirty seconds

When: Every hour at a desk, After a long drive, When you notice tension

How: Hands on the wheel.: Feel the texture and the grip. Back against the seat.: Let the seat take your weight. One deeper breath.: Long and slow out. Notice one thing outside.: A colour, a tree, the sky. Then drive on.

Why it works: Turns dead time into a reset.: Red lights happen anyway. Using them builds a calm habit into your day without extra time. Driving stress builds up.: Small resets stop it stacking up into road rage or arriving frazzled.

Helps with: Arrive calmer, No extra time needed, Builds a habit

When: Every red light, Traffic jams, Before a stressful arrival

How: Choose your object.: A smooth stone, a fidget, a scrap of soft fabric. Keep it on you.: Pocket, bag, car. Rub it when you drift.: Feel the texture with your thumb, slowly. Pair it with a breath.: Rub and breathe out at the same time.

Why it works: An anchor you can carry.: Over time your brain links that texture with calm, so just touching it starts to settle you. Fidgeting is regulating.: For neurodivergent brains, repetitive sensory input helps focus and calm. This is a fidget with a purpose.

Helps with: Always with you, Discreet, Helps you focus

How: Pick a scent you love.: A roller oil, hand cream or perfume. Something that means calm to you. Breathe it in slowly.: A long, slow inhale through your nose. Hold the moment.: Notice where you feel it and what it reminds you of. Long breath out.: Repeat two or three times.

Why it works: Smell is the fastest route to your feelings.: Smell signals go straight to the emotion and memory centres of your brain, without the usual detour. Train a calm association.: Use the same scent when you’re calm (like before bed) and it becomes a shortcut back to that feeling.

Helps with: Works in seconds, Easy to carry, Builds a calm shortcut

When: Anxious moments, Before sleep, Overwhelming places

How: Breathe in through your nose.: A comfortable, slow breath. Hum one low note.: Lips together, “mmmmm”. Feel the buzz.: In your chest, throat, lips and face. Low notes buzz more. Repeat for a minute.: Make the hum as long as is comfortable.

Why it works: Works the vagus nerve directly.: Your vagus nerve runs through your throat, and humming gently stimulates it. Forces a long exhale.: You can’t hum and breathe in, so every hum is a long breath out.

Helps with: Calms you fast, Lifts your mood, Clears your sinuses

When: In the car, In the shower, When your chest feels tight

How: Start brushing.: Same as always. Sway side to side.: Gently shift your weight from foot to foot. Focus on the brush.: Feel it run over each tooth, one by one. Two minutes, done.: Mindfulness without adding a single minute to your day.

Why it works: Rhythmic swaying is soothing.: Gentle side-to-side rocking is one of the oldest calming signals there is. It’s how we settle babies. Habit stacking.: Pairing it with something you already do every day means you’ll actually do it.

Green: recharges me (movement, fun, breathing, connection). Red: drains me fast (highly stimulating, lots of peopling, intense focus, fast pace). Yellow: drains me slowly (medium pace, focus, deep thinking). Pink: neutral or disassociating (scrolling, autopilot; keeps you where you are). Every hour of red needs about 30 minutes of recharge, every hour of yellow about 20.

Money doesn’t create our patterns, it reveals them. Two people can have exactly the same money and completely different realities. Money is neutral. Awareness before change: you can’t rewrite a program you don’t know is running.

entries.t: The three energetic states of money
entries.b: 1. Spending impulsively: money comes in and goes straight out, because holding it doesn’t feel safe (the dropped hot potato). 2. Gripping: all your safety poured into money, a very high floor, a big secret savings account. 2b. The cycle: spend, feel guilty, overcorrect into gripping (feast and famine). 3. Flow: money comes and goes, is enjoyed, and moves like a consistent wave.
Your floor is the minimum balance you won’t let yourself drop below. Your ceiling is the upper limit on what you can hold. Both are settings on the same system.

Money is a hot potato straight out of the oven. Put the mitts on so you can hold it longer: smell it, plate it, butter it, add the toppings, eat it and love every second. Then it’s gone, and that’s fine, because you enjoyed it. It builds the capacity to hold money and the permission to spend it, in one image. Storing money to build it is different from gripping it out of fear.

Money can be made through force (lassoing it and dragging it towards you) or through flow and magnetism, where you stay grounded and money comes to you because it wants to be around you. Effort is a state; deception is an ethics question. They are different things.

Give money a colour, shape, texture, sound and temperature. Is it still or moving? Read your description back to see where you sit with money, then shift one quality at a time towards a happier picture. Sav’s own: warm, yellow, radiant, the sound of slot machines or people celebrating, can’t sit still, always morphing. If it won’t come, remember the last time you were excited to receive money, even for a second.
80% belief, 20% action. Be is the belief, Do is the action, Have is the goal. Become them by doing what they do and you will have what they have.
“I can’t afford it” becomes “How could I?”. Cost vs price vs investment. When did you outsource your self-worth or safety to money? Money likes to move: we save to spend.

The brain isn’t broken. What gets in the way is the conditioning and the trauma layered on top of being neurodivergent: the programs, beliefs and protective habits picked up along the way. That’s the part we rewire.

entries.b: It goes through the body: breathe, find where the feeling sits physically, and let it move rather than talking around it. Imagery (energy, light, sound) and feeling a situation from each person’s side are part of the process.
